Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was preparing to conclude my remarks with respect to the Canadian National Railways, but I realized it would be unfair to the minister if I did so because he would have to start to reply in perhaps a moment or two, which would not have given him an opportunity to deal with the matter. So out of consideration for him, a consideration which I have shown many times in the past, I carried on until five o'clock. I shall occupy the time of the house for only a moment or two more.
I have dealt with various matters affecting the operations of the Canadian National. There are of course many other matters to be dealt with at this time, but they can be dealt with in committee. Unfortunately I will not be present during the sittings of the committee and shall have to leave this to my colleagues, who I am sure will raise these matters.
There is one matter on which I should like to comment before concluding, and I realize that this has often been a cause of rising blood pressure on the part of the minister in the past. I want him to understand at this time that this matter is not being dealt with facetiously, it is being dealt with seriously. Sometimes when the minister thinks I am being facetious he drops his rapier and reaches behind for his bludgeon. He is generally more effective with his rapier than with his bludgeon.
I should like to refer for one moment to the William Carson. I am not going to do this in the way in which I have referred to it in the past, as I am sure this matter will be dealt with in the committee when the minister, Mr. Gordon, and the Canadian National officials will have a field day in which they can explain what has happened, what is happening and what is likely to happen in connection with this ferry. I suggest seriously to the minister that if it should transpire that it is not possible to operate the ferry as had been envisaged when the matter was first considered, if in other words we are going to see next summer a repetition
12, 1957	2133
Committee on Railways and Shipping of what we went through last summer, in view of the fact that the Bluenose now operating between Bar Harbor and Yarmouth is doing such a remarkably good job but is being taxed to its limit, it might be possible to take the William Carson off its present run and put it on that service to supplement the service being provided by the Bluenose.
I know the minister will welcome any favourable comment I can make with respect to the Bluenose. I want to be fair, because I believe they have finally overcome all the difficulties they encountered including missing worm gears, twisted propellers and so on. That boat is doing a remarkably good job between Nova Scotia and Maine.
I feel that credit should be given where credit is due and I want to commend the minister upon the reduction in rates on trucks that was made in answer to the pleas which were heard in the house last year, and which enabled Nova Scotia farm products to be carried to the New England states and possibly on to Ontario and Quebec at lower rates than prevailed during the summer. My one criticism would be that the rates were put into effect too late in the season. It may be that the minister will have the figures in front of him and will be able to say that the reduction did not result in increased business and that the department is not impressed with the arguments which were made. When the rates were lowered I think the minister said it was to be an experiment and he would wait to see the results. I hope the results are satisfactory to the department.
I would urge that this be repeated this year, but that the reduction in rates be inaugurated at an earlier period in the season. If the department is disappointed because of the amount of business obtained through the reduction I would suggest to the minister, without wanting to transgress on the jurisdiction of either the Minister of Finance or-the Minister of Agriculture, that there is a really complicated problem being encountered in the sale of agricultural products in the United States market because of the-premium on the Canadian dollar.
I am sure some of us were shocked to read-today that an all-time high had been reached, It is not particularly profitable to ship farm products into the United States with that premium and receive United States dollars. The result has been that this type of business has not been as profitable to the farmer as ordinarily it would be. But I do contend that the minister and the department deserve credit for having inaugurated this experiment. I am anxious to hear what the minister will say when he speaks later this evening.

Committee on Railways and Shipping
There is only one other matter I wish to refer to in passing, and this will be done very briefly. I may be slightly out of order, as perhaps this does not come within the ambit of this committee. We are all very much concerned about the recommendation of the Gordon commission that there be an inquiry into the transportation facilities of the maritimes and into the Maritime Freight Rates Act. This is not the time to discuss this in detail, but it is a most vital problem to the maritimes at the moment. The operation of the Canadian National Railways during the present or in future years must be predicated upon the results of such inquiries and the legislation which may be brought in as a result.
A definite recommendation has been made that the whole transportation problem of the maritime provinces be investigated, and that recommendation should be implemented immediately. This is something which vitally affects the minister's department and the Canadian National Railways, and I think it should be at least borne in mind when this committee is set up. I am sure many inquiries will be made in committee of the departmental officials, Mr. Gordon and others as to what can be done in that regard.
I think that concludes the comments I want to make at this time. As I said, there are many things that could be raised, but most of them can be dealt with in a detailed way in the committee. I am sure that as it has in the past, this committee will serve a most useful purpose by its inquiry into the operations of the railway system and the steamship lines, and will make recommendations which I hope will be implemented at least in part to the good of the people of the maritimes.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING OWNED, OPERATED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those who have spoken on this resolution which has to do with the transportation companies owned and operated by the government. I would like to go along with some of the remarks made by other hon. members who have spoken, including the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) in connection with the policy which has been adopted. Western Ontario and this part of Canada owes its development down through the years to the railroads that go to make up that great organization, the Canadian National Railways. I well remember the feeling that was stirred up last year when it was said that the mail contracts were going to be taken away from most of the railroads in our district, because so many of the people felt this was the thin end of the wedge-by the way, these mail contracts represented almost one-third
IMr. Nowlan.]
of the total revenue of those railroads-and that eventually the railroads would all be shut off and the lines to Kincardine and Southampton would be abandoned.
In that district we have many urban municipalities which are hoping that one day this idea of decentralizing industry and such things will lead to American and British companies coming to Canada and setting up new industries in these communities. I could cite many advantages in doing so, such as better living conditions and labour conditions that would be advantageous to companies doing that, and it would also be of great benefit to the railroad. I understand that the railroads do have a department to try to decentralize industry, to send industry out to districts such as that in which I live so these smaller communities may benefit from the advantage of having factories in their areas; but if these railroad lines are abandoned, and the service is cut off, the chances of these communities ever getting industry is pretty well done away with because most industries of any size demand a rail service.
In connection with some of the services that have been cut off, I may say they have cut off the passenger service from Palmerston to Durham. For two weeks they ran the same train with the same crew at the same time; but the caboose fell apart, or something. They put the same coach back on that mixed train and ran it up and down over that line with the same crew, but they would not let any of the people who went down to the station get on the coach and ride as passengers.
I don't know whether that is good public relations or what it is, but there were a few people who would have liked to travel on that train; the coach was there, and I don't see why they were not allowed to travel. Having been raised in a small railroad centre which, I can remember, was a very busy centre at one time with hundreds of men working in the freight sheds and in the shops, I naturally regret that this should have dwindled to a mere handful of men carrying on this work, and I find myself asking why the railroads should have lost all that business. I sometimes feel, as the hon. member for Perth indicated he felt, that if the railways improved the service up there they could get back a lot of the business in that district.
I was reading an article in a Canadian national magazine that came to our desks yesterday about a new train they were investigating in Sweden called the "Kort, Lag and Latt"-"Short, low and light"-and in this article it says:
The story behind the KLL is a familiar one. Alarmed by diminishing passenger returns, the state

railways took a hard second look at existing rolling stock, found that it had grown too fat and frilly.
After all, I do feel that if the railroads improved the service and gave a more specialized service they could get back a lot of this business. The final paragraph of this article says this:
With a polite bow in the direction of other lightweight builders, the Swedes are careful to say that the KLL is custom-built for local conditions inside a country that is only slightly bigger than the state of California, where quick turnaround and a flexible consist become of paramount importance.
But they make no secret of their belief that they've gone a step further-and in the right direction-than anybody else in the lightweight field.
I sometimes wonder how much investigation and research is being done by the railroads in this connection. We have heard about the trains that are being used on some of the branch lines and which are giving wonderful service, and I feel that if they were adopted more universally on branch lines many more people would travel on them. As the hon. member for Perth indicated, people are not too happy about driving their cars from outlying districts into the city of Toronto today because of traffic and parking conditions, and if they could get good service from the railroads I believe many people would go back to that type of transportation.
The railroads may say that the passenger service provides only a small part of the revenue, but I feel this is the same as any other kind of business; you don't make 100 per cent profit on everything you do. Yesterday we were talking about public relations with regard to a bill which was before the house, and I sometimes feel that if the railroads took this question of public relations more seriously they would do better. Sometimes they do not seem to realize that a man travelling in one of these old coaches may be a furniture manufacturer with a factory in one of these areas, and after one of these rides in not too pleasant circumstances he may say, "If this is the kind of service they are going to give me, my freight is going by road".
There is another idea that occurs to me, and that is with regard to a circular that came in today concerning "piggyback" transportation. I do feel that is something which could be given a great deal of research and investigation by the railroads. It is being used now from Toronto to Montreal, and it might become more universal. If we look at its origin, it seems that away back in 1855 the Halifax-Truro railway, a line built by the Nova Scotia government, inaugurated "piggyback" for the transportation of farmers' wagons.
A lot of the business that used to go on in the community where I lived was concerned
Committee on Railways and Shipping with stock. At 5.30 every day a stock train went out of that town, stock that had been brought in on the branch lines. That business is all being carried by truck today. Perhaps if the railroad went into this "piggyback" business some arrangement could be made whereby these stock trucks could be carried "piggyback" to Toronto and be moved from there to the stockyards.
However, I do feel that the railroads have an important place in the life of these smaller communities, and I hope the railroad companies will consider the suggestions I have made and take a second look at these small branch lines, because they mean a great deal to the people in those districts.

There are two controversies at the present time in our district. Our people are fighting, and I think rightly so. I was at a meeting in Wiarton about two months ago. The people there were stirred up like a hive of bees, and I think they were right. We have another controversy now about cutting off the Tara station in Bruce. The discontinuance of the carrying of mail on the trains is the thin edge of the wedge, but in order to put something over on the people of Bruce the wedge will have to be a lot thinner.
I should like to say that the board of transport commissioners is doing a real good job. Considering the way the railway has been trying to make use of the board in Bruce, we are very thankful that the board is there. I have faith that the board will continue to act in the manner understood they should when the board was established to do this work, and to see that people get railway service. Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two. On a number of occasions I have said that when buying new freight cars the C.N.R. should insist that the cars have a light line along their sides so people driving motor cars at night will be able to see the freight cars and not run into them, as has happened week after week, month after month through the years, with dozens of people being killed. It would not cost the C.N.R. any additional money, and it would result in people definitely being able to see the freight cars. At present these cars are a dull, dirt colour that blends into the landscape, and on a dark, foggy night it is almost impossible to see them until you are right into them.
I know the minister has had the experience of squinting at freight cars from his automobile. All you can see is the light in the cab of the engine; you cannot see the cars. I know this is being done on some of the railways in the United States. They are putting light coloured lines on their freight cars. The C.N.R. could do the same, and on the coloured Strip or above it they could advertise Canada. I think it would be a safety measure for the protection of motorists in general, and would create a lot of good will for the C.N.R.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to confirm what my seatmate has just said. When coming to Toronto last winter something ran into the side of the train I was on. There was only one coach, an express car and the engine, and something ran into the express car ahead of us. We knew we had run over something. The train did not stop, but when we got down the line a little farther it was reported that we had killed a man who had run into the side of the train with a pick-up truck. It was about half past seven in the morning, before daylight, and there is no doubt in the world that the driver did not see the train at all. Of course, the engineer did not see him because he was past the point of impact. The driver of the truck drifted right into
[Mr. Robinson (Bruce) .1

the side of the train. He hit the express coach in the vicinity of the door. A light line on the side of the train in that case might have done a lot of good.
Before I sit down I should like to confirm what other hon. members have said. In my section of the country the railway has been threatening to take off train service. On our line last summer the railway operated an old colonist coach that has been on the road for 75 years, I suppose. It was the old style of sleeper used in the past for excursions to the west. The bunks were not turned down, but they were still there. That is the kind of car we had to travel in all last summer. It was not so bad in the winter because it was nice and warm, but in the summer you could not open the windows and the only way you could get fresh air was through the door. That is one reason the C.N.R. are not getting any passenger traffic, simply because they are not giving any service to the general public.
I should also like to mention the fact that the mail was taken off the trains last year. We tried our best to have it kept on the trains but it was claimed that it could be hauled much cheaper by truck. That may be true. I am not complaining about the present mail service, but I am complaining that the purpose in taking the mail off the train was so the railway would have the excuse that the train was not paying its way. The next move will be to try to take the train off the line, because that is exactly what they tried to do the year before although they did not get away with it.
I do not know what you are going to do with the main lines if you discontinue all the feeder lines. There is one thing that is sure: If you do not keep the feeder lines to feed the main lines, it will not be long until the main lines will be gone too, and what are you going to do then?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING OWNED, OPERATED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to attempt to deal with all the many points that have come out during the course of the discussion we have had this afternoon and evening on this motion for the setting up of a committee in connection with the accounts and estimates of the Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. I think, however, there are one or two points with which I should like to deal.
There has been during the debate a good deal of comment with regard to the abandonment of rail service in different parts of the country, particularly in western Ontario. During the course of the discussion itself it appeared and it was made quite clear by the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe who has just resumed his seat -that the great difficulty of the railroads in the day in which we live is that there is a certain natural competition which it is difficult for them to meet. It is difficult to meet because the competing modes of transport offer advantages which the railway is quite unable to offer.
A moment ago the hon. member for Lapointe mentioned the facility with which the people in his part of the country can reach Quebec when travelling by road, and the fact that they could do so more rapidly than when they travelled by train. We who drive motor cars from time to time know that if you have a relatively short distance to go, if you are going by automobile you leave when you feel like it. You are not bound to respect the schedule of passenger services which the railroads must obviously adopt. Consequently there is a very natural tendency for individuals with motor cars to make use of those cars, and of the highways in the region in which they live, to travel short distances. We all know that for short distances it is difficult for trains to compete with the automobile.

The same remarks apply to the situation with respect to transportation by truck. It is a fact that under many circumstances it is much more convenient for the shipper of goods to send them to their destination by truck than it is to send them by rail. I do not think any serious-minded person would dispute the fact that very often service by truck offers advantages which the railway is quite unable to offer. There is the very obvious fact that there is only one handling of the goods into the truck and out of the truck when the goods are loaded by the shipper and unloaded at destination.
Everyone, I believe, should realize that this type of competition is virtually impossible for the railway to meet, regardless of its name and whether it be owned by the people of Canada or by private capital. I think that is the situation all over the North American continent. I do not believe there is any use beating our breasts and saying that the railways should make greater efforts to get back some of this business, because some of it has been lost irrevocably as a result of the fact that truck transportation often offers a better, more efficient and cheaper way of getting goods from the point of shipment to destination.
There is another fact which I think people should recognize in connection with the type of competition for passenger business which is offered by buses and by private automobiles, and the competition for the highly valued goods which quite definitely move by truck. That is that these are conveniences which we are quite prepared to accept. We should not, therefore, having accepted these conveniences, then proceed to criticize the fact that the railways are no longer able to offer on an economic basis the services they did offer when these forms of competition did not exist. I think we should be realistic about it and realize we cannot have our cake and eat it too.
Really, what is the long-term history of many of these branch lines? I am not going to reach too far back into history, because I know what I am going to say does not apply in all cases. So often when it comes to building a branch line the community is overjoyed if the railway will build the line. Very often it is the fact that the railway has built the line that has given birth to the community and assisted its development. Then when the community prospers and its industries are set up, the first thing you know you have an excellent highway. The business of the community then begins to be divided between the railway and the trucks. The first thing you know the trucks are carrying most of it and the passengers go by automobile and by bus. speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members will find that this is indeed a very simple bill. The purpose of the bill, as its title suggests, is to amend the Canada Shipping Act, and specifically section 493. That section provides for the general penalty in respect of violations of any of the provisions of part VII of the act, which deals with the subject of steamship inspection.
I think hon. members will understand the situation better if I read the terms of section 493, which are as follows:
Except where otherwise specially provided in this part, the owner or master of any Canadian ship is liable to a fine not exceeding $100 and not less than $50 for any violation of any provision of this part or regulation made thereunder.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, the use of the words "a Canadian ship", which in the act is defined in section 2 to mean a ship registered in Canada. In this connection I would remind hon. members that ships of less than 15 tons burden do not require to be registered, so it will be readily apparent that these particular Canadian ships are not subject to this penalty provision of section 493 which I have just read.
The deputy minister of justice has expressed the view that section 493 does not extend to offences committed by ships other than ships registered in Canada, and an amendment of the act is required before the regulations made under part VII may be enforced by prosecution against unregistered vessels.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the regulations for which a penalty ought to be provided are made in Canada, and those that apply to those unregistered vessels, which obviously are small craft, are: first, the fire detection and extinguishing equipment regulations; second, regulations regarding life-saving appliances; and, third, small fishing vessel inspection regulations.
The purpose of this bill is to extend the scope of section 493 of the act to cover violations by unregistered vessels of any provisions of part VII of the act or of the regulations made under part VII of the act.

I must say that I have read this bill, and I took from it something entirely different from that which the minister has explained. Canada Shipping Act
anything of that sort is also involved in this bill, which will change the reference from "Canadian ship" to "any ship".
There is this whole question of the safety regulations in respect of ships. The minister mentioned the steamship section. As I understand it, part VII also applies to the inspection of ships tackle and the safety measures that are now required to safeguard those who are loading and unloading ships in Canadian ports. Those are all matters of considerable interest.
I have looked through part VII, and I notice that many of the sections thereof provide specific penalties. It is a little difficult for one reading the act to decide to what sections this ammended penalty clause would apply. I am wondering if the minister intends to refer this bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where we would have an opportunity to discuss it with the experts from the department.
The minister will recall that last year we had what I considered was a most valuable discussion on a proposal having to do with the licensing of small boats. During that time we also had an opportunity of discussing some of the safety regulations which now exist in regard to providing fire extinguishers and so on, which the minister has mentioned. I take it that the proposals contained in this bill arise in part from the increased interest in ensuring an observance of proper safety measures by the owners of small craft which ply our waters.
I hope the minister will keep in mind the idea of sending this bill to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines so we may have an opportunity of obtaining information in much more detail than we can possibly obtain it on the floor of the house. Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything at this time, as I had expected to deal with what I have in mind during the committee stage; but in view of the fact that hon. members who have preceded me have raised some points, I should like to ask the minister to explain the connection between sections 493 and 494 of the Canada Shipping Act. Section 493, which is the section to be amended by this bill, seems to be a general penalty section, presumably to provide penalties not contained in other sections of this particular act. Section 494 is headed "Special applications of this part" which is referring to the whole of part VII. Subsection 1 reads:
The governor in council may direct that this part or any of the provisions thereof shall apply to any ship or class of ship registered elsewhere than in Canada whilst within the territorial waters of Canada.
That seems to make it possible to extend the provisions of that part to all foreign ships in Canadian waters, including the provisions of section 493, the general penalty section. Subsection 2 of section 494 reads:
This part applies to all unregistered ships, other than ships belonging to Her Majesty and government ships, whilst they are within Canada.
That subsection would seem to be wide enough to make part VII, including the general penalty section, applicable to all unregistered ships. If I am correct in my interpretation of section 494 there would seem to be no need for deleting the word "Canadian" in section 493. The situation may not be just as I have expressed it, but on reading those two sections it would seem to me that the department already has the power under section 494 to do everything that would be done by deleting the word "Canadian" in section 493.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has described properly the purpose of section 494. The very words of the section confirm the opinion the hon. member has just expressed. The heading of section 493 is "General penalty" and it reads:
Except where otherwise specially provided in this part, the owner or master of any Canadian ship is liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars for any violation of any provision of this part of regulation made thereunder.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni indicated, there are specific sections in part VII where a penalty is indicated. This is a general penalty clause which applies to those regulations where a penalty is not specifically spelled out, and to those sections of the act which require something to be done but for which no specific penalty is enacted.
TMr. Hahn.]
The only difficulty which arises is that although at first sight it would appear that there is no division between sections 493 and 494, the deputy minister of justice has expressed the view that this general penalty clause does not apply to ships not registered in Canada, that is to say ships under 15 tons. As I said before, the expression "Canadian ship" is defined by section 2 of the act as meaning a ship registered in Canada. We have the rather curious position that the general penalty clause refers only to ships which are registered, and it would only be by means of section 494(2) that unregistered ships might conceivably be made subject to the provisions of section 493.
I have not attempted to go into the matter particularly because I think section 493 was enacted by the house under the impression that its provisions extended to all Canadian ships, whether registered or not, and that the combination of sections 493 and 494 would attain that objective. The fact is that the legislation has not succeeded in achieving that end, and the sole purpose of the legislation is to make it perfectly clear that all ships will be subject to the provisions of the general penalty clause.
The question was raised whether this was going to affect vessels other than Canadian ships, and I would merely point out to the house that section 494, in subsection 1, provides expressly:
The governor in council may direct that this part or any of the provisions thereof shall apply to any ship or class of ship registered elsewhere than in Canada whilst within the territorial waters of Canada.
So these foreign vessels are not being made subject to the general penalty clause by the draft amendment which we are now considering but, rather, are made subject to it under section 494, which I have iust read.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might add one word: I was not proposing to send this bill to the committee because the subject matter is really very simple. It was -considered in the other place and was not found to be contentious. In committee of the whole, if there are other questions which hon. members wish to ask I would have members of my staff here, and I am sure the committee will be informed regarding anything they may wish to know.

speechtext: I can appreciate the minister's remarks with respect to this matter. I have been following the discussion, and I have taken the trouble to look up the definition given to the term "ship" in the definition section of the act. Then while we are considering this clause we would also be able to come to an understanding whether, for example, the penalty that is set forth as the maximum penalty is an appropriate one to carry forward into the proposed new section. As I understand it, there is not any proposal to change it from the old one, but I think it would be useful for us to get some idea as to what type of offence this penalty applies to, in contrast to the penalties which are provided under the other penalty sections of this part of the act.
One of the parts of the act in which I have a particular interest, because it does affect the people who live in my district, are those sections which apply to regulations for ships' tackle, the part which provides that certain safety measures will be observed in respect to the loading and unloading of ships. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sorry if I seem to be repeating myself too often, but I find a certain repetition in the substance of the questions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think that is an understatement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS

The hon. member for Kootenay West may be quite right; it may be an understatement. In the first place, the question of the definition of any ship is a question that was raised in the other place but was not considered to be of any particular moment. After all, what we are really concerned with here are the regulations, and we all know that the regulations are not designed to regulate the conduct of people in canoes, dugouts or rowboats. These regulations are designed to protect the lives of people who are engaged in activities of one kind or another on the water; they are safety regulations.
The point I have been trying to make since the beginning of the evening is this. When section 493 as it is now to be found in the Canada Shipping Act was first enacted,

everybody believed that section applied to all offences under part VII of the act for which a specific penalty had not been enacted. I know the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will have no difficulty, if he will refer to part VII, in finding specific sections in which the penalty is indicated. All he has to do is open the shipping act at any page to find examples of that. However, so far as the regulations themselves are concerned, and so far as perhaps a few sections in part VII are concerned, there is no penalty, and that is why we need this clause which appears under the heading of "general penalty". The general penalty was thought to apply to all vessels to which part VII applies. Unfortunately a magistrate in Ontario has told us it does not apply to ships owned by Canadians which are not subject to registration. The purpose is to correct that situation in order that section 493 will in fact more effectively translate the will of parliament when section 493 was originally enacted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION OF SAFETY REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member's
impression is correct. The regulations do not carry a penalty and the penalty is provided for in this general penalty clause, section 493.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 225, to amend the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act was passed
Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation in 1947, and confirmed an agreement with Alberta whereby federal assistance would be extended for capital and maintenance works on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains in Alberta. The act and the agreement were amended in 1952. The amendment now proposed is of a simple nature. The first change is to authorize the official audit of the board's expenditures to be made by the provincial auditor rather than by the Auditor General of Canada. As all maintenance costs are borne by the provincial government of Alberta, and as Canada's capital contributions have been completed, this is a logical change.
The original agreement and the amendment of 1952 both set certain limitations on the maintenance program with the intention of ensuring that a program of reasonable size was carried out. It is now considered that the board's work has reached the stage where no specific limitations should be imposed, particularly in view of the fact that the province is entirely responsible for maintenance costs. The second change in the amendment now being proposed would amend these limitations.
A third change deals with fire-fighting costs. The original agreement provided that if the board's forest fire-fighting costs exceeded $10,000 in any year, the excess would be borne on an equal share basis by the two governments. Both the federal government and Alberta agree that this provision should be eliminated, in view of the recent offer made under the Canada Forestry Act of federal assistance to all Canadian provinces in forest fire protection. The proposed amendment would delete this provision which is out of line with, and to some extent duplicates, the new federal offer.
The last change proposed, sir, is in section 20(b) of the original agreement. This subsection provided that all property of the board, apart from improvements, works and land, would belong to the federal government on the expiration of the agreement. As the agreement does not expire until at least 1973, and federal capital contributions ended in 1955, all items covered by the subsection and toward which federal contributions had been made would almost certainly have depreciated to the point where they were almost valueless. As the board's work will be a continuing provincial responsibility, it seems reasonable to amend the subsection to provide that the items in question should belong to the province on the expiration of the agreement; that is, in 1973.

maintopic: EASTERN ROCKY MOUNTAIN FOREST CONSERVATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING METHOD OF AUDITING EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that this bill has been brought in consequent upon the fact that the agreement between the dominion and the

Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation province of Alberta in regard to the eastern Rocky mountain forest conservation scheme has come to an end as far as the financial contribution of the dominion government is concerned.
The scheme was an extraordinarily good one. I think everyone who had any knowledge of conditions there and of the advantages which might be secured by putting into operation that scheme of reforesting the eastern slope was delighted that this agreement was entered into, and particularly pleased with the way in which the activities of this board were carried on.
In connection with that I should like to pay tribute particularly to General Kennedy, who was the dominion representative and chairman of that board. I am only sorry that the activities of the board were not extended somewhat farther north. It is true that in that area north of the point where the board's activities came to an end the forest cover had not been destroyed to the same extent as in the area where it operated; nevertheless I think it would have been to the advantage of the dominion as well as to the advantage of the province if the scheme had been extended somewhat farther north, particularly to take in the area north of the line from Edmonton to Jasper national park.
The work of this board having been so satisfactory, and I think of so much benefit, particularly as far as the future is concerned, to the prairie provinces generally, I would hope that further joint ventures of the dominion and the provinces along this line might be initiated.

maintopic: EASTERN ROCKY MOUNTAIN FOREST CONSERVATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING METHOD OF AUDITING EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we consider that recently the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources started about 9.30 with his estimates and brought in another bill at about 9.30, and now gets a chance with this bill at about 10 minutes to 10, I suppose it would be correct to call him the minister of late starts. Anyway, he has been very patiently sitting there waiting for the opportunity to go on.
The Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act was a very important piece of legislation passed in 1947, a much more valuable and important piece of legislation than many members of this house realized and than many people across the country realize even today. I understand it was passed as a result of the consideration of the depletion of the natural resources of the area concerned, the particularly vital interest of the federal government in the maintenance of the river flows from the eastern rocky mountain slopes through the
TMr. Harknes".]
prairie provinces, and the desire on the part of the federal government to see that those flows were maintained.
Therefore in the first instance this legislation was of great importance to all the prairie provinces, and as a result has been of great importance to Canada as a whole.
Personally I think it is an excellent example of successful and effective co-operation between the federal government and the province of Alberta in the practice of conservation, development and utilization of natural resources. I believe it is an example that should be a good guide to future action.
Before proceeding I would also like to pay a tribute to Major General Kennedy, who has been chairman of this board since its inception. During war and peace he has demonstrated his ability as a most efficient administrator and engineer, and in connection with this work a most qualified forest engineer. He is a well-trained person with long experience; but more than that, General Kennedy has the feel for the conservation of natural resources. You must have not only training and experience. There are only certain individuals who have the capacity to, shall I say, get the feel of the situation and know what should be undertaken for the protection or development of certain natural resources. This scheme represents one of the first instances in Canada on any scale of unified scientific management.
I understand that under this board the resources of the whole area are controlled. There is control of prospecting for oil and other resources. There is control and planning of recreation, control of game resources, of fish resources, control of trapping licences, and then control of the forest resources. I understand there has been forest protection and forest management and investigation and control with respect to insects and pests. That is the conservation aspect of the controls so far as forest management is concerned. At the same time I understand there is control of the logging operation within the area. The board sells the timber under its jurisdiction in the right manner, and at the right time, and see that it is harvested in the proper way. I understand that last year something like 65 million board feet of timber were cut within this area, and at the same time about 2.75 million lineal feet of poles, fence posts and round timbers, and things of that type.
In addition, I understand the board has control of range management, undertakes renting and leasing for grazing purposes, and also has complete control of watershed management. Here is an area, as the result of co-operation between the federal government and the provincial government, which

is being scientifically managed and those resources scientifically conserved, developed and utilized.

speechtext:
I.	During 1956, did the Department of National Defence learn that certain records of the Longue Pointe ordnance depot in Montreal were allegedly falsified so that certain employees received wages for time during which they were absent from work?
2.	If so, what action was taken regarding the cases disclosed?
3.	What steps have been taken to prevent a recurrence of this practice?
Answer by: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	Yes.
2.	The employees found responsible for falsifying the timekeeping records were dismissed.
3.	Steps are being taken with a view to modernizing the present timekeeping devices in the area and in the meantime closer supervision is being maintained over employees entering and leaving the depot.
